questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Challenges of Nation-Building' refers to.
questions.a: Nation-building refers to the process of bringing the people of a newly independent country together under a single political identity and a shared sense of belonging, while establishing stable democratic institutions and addressing problems of unity, development, and democracy.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Challenges of Nation-Building'.
questions.a: After independence in 1947, India faced three major challenges of nation-building: shaping a united nation, establishing democracy, and ensuring development and welfare for all citizens.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Challenges of Nation-Building' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Introduction to Nation-Building

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Partition and its Aftermath' refers to.
questions.a: The Partition of India in 1947 was the division of British India into two independent dominions, India and Pakistan, on the basis of the two-nation theory, accompanied by large-scale communal violence, mass migration, and enormous human suffering.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Partition and its Aftermath'.
questions.a: Partition was the result of the two-nation theory advocated by the Muslim League; it caused one of the largest mass migrations in history and left a legacy of communal tension and unresolved disputes between India and Pakistan.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Partition and its Aftermath' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Partition of India

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Integration of Princely States' refers to.
questions.a: The integration of princely states was the process by which over 500 princely states, which were not directly under British rule, were merged into the Indian Union after independence, through persuasion, referendums, and in some cases military action.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Integration of Princely States'.
questions.a: At independence there were over 500 princely states; the Indian leadership, led by Sardar Patel, used a combination of diplomacy, incentives, and force to integrate almost all of them into the Indian Union.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Integration of Princely States' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Integration of Princely States

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Sardar Patel and Integration' refers to.
questions.a: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, India's first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister, played a central role in the integration of princely states by persuading and pressuring their rulers to accede to the Indian Union, thereby securing the territorial unity of India.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Sardar Patel and Integration'.
questions.a: Sardar Patel used a combination of diplomacy, the appeal to patriotism, and the threat of force to integrate over 500 princely states into the Indian Union, earning him the title 'Iron Man of India'.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Sardar Patel and Integration' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Role of Sardar Patel

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Nehru's Approach to Nation-Building' refers to.
questions.a: Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first Prime Minister, shaped the nation-building approach through his commitment to democracy, secularism, planned economic development, non-alignment in foreign policy, and the modern scientific temper.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Nehru's Approach to Nation-Building'.
questions.a: Nehru's approach to nation-building emphasised democratic institutions, secularism, planned development through the Planning Commission, a mixed economy, and an independent foreign policy of non-alignment.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Nehru's Approach to Nation-Building' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Nehru's Vision

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Linguistic Reorganisation of States' refers to.
questions.a: The linguistic reorganisation of states was the process of redrawing state boundaries on the basis of language, beginning with the creation of Andhra State in 1953 and formalised by the States Reorganisation Act of 1956, to meet the demand for administrative units based on linguistic identity.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Linguistic Reorganisation of States'.
questions.a: The demand for linguistic states, sparked by the fast unto death of Potti Sriramulu, led to the creation of Andhra in 1953 and the States Reorganisation Act of 1956, which reorganised states on linguistic lines and strengthened national unity.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Linguistic Reorganisation of States' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Linguistic Reorganisation of States

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Tribal Integration' refers to.
questions.a: Tribal integration refers to the policy of bringing tribal communities into the mainstream of national life while protecting their culture and identity, through special constitutional provisions, scheduled areas, and development programmes.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Tribal Integration'.
questions.a: India adopted a policy of protective integration of tribal communities through constitutional safeguards (Fifth and Sixth Schedules), reserved seats, and development schemes, rather than forcing assimilation.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Tribal Integration' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Tribal Integration

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Northeast India and Integration' refers to.
questions.a: The integration of Northeast India involved bringing the diverse tribal and non-tribal communities of the region into the Indian Union through the Sixth Schedule, state reorganisation, and special arrangements, while addressing demands for autonomy and separatism.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Northeast India and Integration'.
questions.a: Northeast India, with its ethnic diversity and distance from the mainland, posed special challenges of integration; these were addressed through the Sixth Schedule, creation of new states, and special provisions, though some demands for autonomy and separatism persisted.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Northeast India and Integration' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Northeast India

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Challenges to Democracy' refers to.
questions.a: The challenges to democracy in the early years of independent India included conducting the first general elections based on universal adult franchise, building democratic institutions, managing political competition, and ensuring the participation of a largely illiterate population in the democratic process.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Challenges to Democracy'.
questions.a: India chose to establish democracy immediately after independence, conducting the first general elections in 1951-52 on the basis of universal adult franchise, which was a bold and unprecedented experiment given the scale and diversity of the country.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Challenges to Democracy' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Challenges to Democracy
